passages.t: The LORD comes down, and Samaria's ruin
passages.happening:
‘This is the word of the LORD that came to Micah the Moreshite in the days of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah, kings of Judah’ (verse 1), what he saw about Samaria and Jerusalem. “Hear, O peoples, all of you; listen, O earth, and everyone in it!” (verse 2). The Lord GOD will be a witness against them from his holy temple.

The LORD comes out of his dwelling and treads on the high places of the earth (verse 3). Mountains melt under him like wax before the fire, and valleys split open (verse 4). All this is for the sin of Jacob. What is Jacob's sin? Samaria. What is Judah's high place? Jerusalem (verse 5). So Samaria will become a heap of rubble in an open field, its stones poured into the valley (verse 6). Its carved images will be smashed and its idols destroyed (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The heading places Micah under three kings of Judah, from the 740s to about 700 BC. The word against Samaria must come before it fell to Assyria in 722 BC.

The picture of God's coming draws on the language used of God's appearing at Sinai and in the psalms: storm, fire and earthquake. High places were hilltop shrines where Israelites often mixed the worship of the LORD with Canaanite practices. Micah shocks his hearers by calling Jerusalem itself Judah's high place.

The wages of a prostitute in verse 7 are the temple treasures Samaria had gathered through worship Micah calls unfaithfulness. Conquerors would carry them off to their own temples, where they would serve false worship again. Micah's hearers probably expected God to come down against Assyria. Instead the verdict falls on Samaria and Jerusalem.
passages.later: The picture of mountains melting before God is also in the psalms: ‘The mountains melt like wax at the presence of the LORD’ (Psalm 97:5). Second Kings tells Samaria's fall (2 Kings 17:5-6).
passages.hard:
Why does God come in judgment against his own people instead of their enemies?

Micah's hearers probably expected God to come against Assyria. Instead the verdict falls on Samaria and Jerusalem. The Old Testament teaches again and again that privilege brings responsibility: the people who knew God's law and bore his name were judged by it. Micah does not say the nations are innocent. They are called as witnesses in verse 2 and judged elsewhere. But he insists that God's people cannot treat their status as protection while practicing idolatry and injustice.

Some readers find the severity troubling. Others note that Micah weeps over the judgment he announces, and that the book promises restoration again and again. Judgment in Micah is real, but it is not God's last word. And it is Israel's own Scripture, spoken by an Israelite prophet to his own people. It is never a reason to blame the Jewish people.
passages.asks: Micah calls the capital city itself the high place of idolatry. Ask where the center of your life has become a place of compromise. And ask whether you have assumed that belonging to God's people protects you from his judgment.

passages.t: A funeral song for the towns near home
passages.happening:
‘Because of this I will lament and wail; I will walk barefoot and naked’ (verse 8). Micah howls like a jackal and mourns like an ostrich, because the wound cannot be healed. It has reached Judah, as far as the gate of Jerusalem (verse 9).

Then he names the towns near his home one by one. Do not tell it in Gath. Roll in the dust in Beth-leaphrah (verse 10). The people of Shaphir go out in shameful nakedness, and those of Zaanan do not come out (verse 11). Maroth waits for good, but disaster comes down from the LORD to the gate of Jerusalem (verse 12). Lachish is told to harness its chariot horses (verse 13). Farewell gifts are sent to Moresheth-gath, and Achzib deceives the kings of Israel (verse 14). A conqueror comes to Mareshah, and the glory of Israel goes to Adullam (verse 15). The people are to shave their heads in mourning for their children, who will go into exile (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Micah mourns with the customs of grief: wailing, going barefoot, stripping off outer garments, cries like the jackals and ostriches whose howls haunted the desert at night. Shaving the head was a common sign of mourning.

The lament is one of the most intricate pieces of wordplay in the prophets. Verse 10 begins with an echo of David's lament for Saul. Then nearly every town's name becomes a pun on its fate. Beth-leaphrah, house of dust, rolls in the dust. Shaphir, beautiful, goes out in shame. Zaanan, which sounds like go out, does not come out. Maroth, bitterness, waits for good. Lachish sounds like the word for horses. Moresheth sounds like betrothed, so it receives farewell gifts, like a bride leaving home. Achzib, deception, deceives. Mareshah sounds like possessor, so a conqueror comes. Every place name becomes an obituary.

The towns lay mostly in the Shephelah, around Micah's home. Many scholars connect the lament with Sennacherib's invasion in 701 BC, when, by his own account, he captured forty-six fortified towns of Judah and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a bird in a cage. Others suggest an earlier Assyrian campaign in the region, around 711 BC under Sargon II. Lachish, the strongest fortress of the Shephelah, fell to Sennacherib; excavations there have uncovered his siege ramp. Adullam was the cave where David hid from Saul.
passages.later: David's lament for Saul began, ‘Tell it not in Gath’ (2 Samuel 1:20). Isaiah too went barefoot and stripped as a sign of coming captivity (Isaiah 20:2-4), and David hid in the cave of Adullam (1 Samuel 22:1).
passages.asks: Micah grieves over the very towns he warns. Ask whether you can speak hard truth and still weep over the people it falls on. And ask which places and people near your own home you carry before God.
